title: throughput-latency-tradeoff-capsule-notes
summary: Notes from an experimental sweep that trades throughput (QPS / batching) against E2E latency quantiles. Focused on isolating stage-level contributions (tokenize -> model infer -> kv cache -> egress) across warm vs cold starts and two hardware classes. Key takeaway: small increases in batch size drastically lower cost/QPS but push p95 into an unacceptable range for latency-sensitive routes; KV hit rate and cold-start tails dominate p99 in low-batching regimes.
body:
Context and motivation:
We ran a targeted trace sweep to characterize how increasing batching and queueing (to raise throughput) affects end-to-end latency quantiles for typical customer payload distributions. This is intended to feed routing policy decisions: which routes can tolerate batching/cost-optimized paths vs routes that need low-latency pinning.

Experiment matrix (short):
- Hardware: A100 (H: a100-80gb), H100 (H: h100-80gb)
- Batching modes: none (batch=1), micro (batch target 4, max wait 10ms), medium (target 8, max wait 25ms), large (target 16, max wait 40ms)
- KV cache hit rate assumptions: high (~95%, synthetic warm workload), mixed (~60%), cold (~0%)
- Cold start surface: zero-worker vs warm pool (kept warm for 60s)
- Workload: mixed prompt lengths: short 20–64 tokens (60%), medium 128–256 (30%), long 512–1024 (10%)
- Measurement: E2E p50/p95/p99, per-stage medians and 95th percentiles (tokenize, preprocess, model infer, kv lookup, batching wait, postprocess/egress). Traces sampled at 10k requests per config.

High-level observations (bullet form):
- Cost vs latency: moving from batch=1 to batch target=8 reduced aggregate token compute cost by ~35% (measured via GPU utilization and tokens/sec), but p95 latency increased from ~120ms to ~340ms on A100 for mixed workload.
- p50 movement is modest; p95 and p99 inflate rapidly due to two factors: batching-induced queue wait and cold-start amplification for long sequences.
- KV cache hit rate strongly gates p99: with 95% hits, p99 dominated by batching wait + model tail; at 0% hits p99 shifts +150–250ms because of cache-miss-dependent deskewing (additional DB/RPCs).
- H100 shows ~20–25% reduction in model-infer time for long sequences vs A100, but the relative p95 impact from batching wait is similar; hardware helps the base infer time but not the queueing tail.

Representative per-stage breakdown (select config snapshots) — plain text lines for traceability:
Config A: A100, batch=1, kv=95%, warm pool
- p50 total: 110ms
- p95 total: 125ms
- p99 total: 180ms
- stage medians: tokenize 6ms, preprocess 9ms, model_infer 80ms, kv_lookup 3ms (hit), egress 12ms
- stage p95: tokenize 18ms, preprocess 25ms, model_infer 105ms, kv_lookup 12ms, egress 28ms

Config B: A100, batch target=8, max_wait=25ms, kv=95%, warm pool
- p50 total: 160ms (batch wait median ~20ms included)
- p95 total: 340ms (batch wait p95 ~140ms; model_infer p95 ~105ms)
- p99 total: 560ms (long seq and some cache misses amplified)
- stage p95 contributions (approx): batching_wait 140ms, model_infer 105ms, egress 28ms

Config C: A100, batch target=8, kv=0% (cold cache), warm pool
- p50 total: 220ms
- p95 total: 520ms
- p99 total: 820ms
- notes: remote KV RPCs add ~180–260ms in miss cases; these stack with batching wait.

Config D: H100, batch target=8, kv=95%, warm pool
- p50 total: 140ms
- p95 total: 270ms
- p99 total: 430ms
- notes: model_infer improved (~70ms p50) vs A100, batching wait similar magnitude.

Cold-start behavior (example): A100, batch=1, cold worker spinup
- p50 total: 240ms
- p95 total: 1.2s
- p99 total: 2.4s
- root causes: container image pull negligible in our infra (warm pool used), but model weights load+GPU init + JIT/optimization paths create heavy p99 tail. Warm pools materially reduce these tails.

Why p95 vs p99 diverge so strongly:
- p95 is dominated by batching wait + model variability for the majority of requests. When queueing is allowed, long waits shift p95 immediately.
- p99 is heavily sensitive to low-frequency events: cold model init, KV miss combined with long-sequence inference, intermittent device GC/stall, and rare egress stalls. These compound multiplicatively.

Implications for routing and SLOs:
- Low-latency routes (chat UI, API-SYNC endpoints) should default to batch=1 or micro-batch with very small max_wait (<=8ms) and warm pool pinning; accept higher cost.
- Throughput-optimized routes (async batch jobs, background embedding pipelines) can use medium/large batching and fall back to cheaper hardware / quantized variants. Provide opt-in for customers to choose cost-latency tier.
- Introduce a runtime knob: quantile_sla which pins max allowed batch_wait for p95 budget. If exceeded, route is auto-failed to low-latency pool.

Trace quality and measurement caveats:
- Sampling bias: we used uniform sampling at ingress but heavy-tailed requests are rarer—need stratified sampling for long-seq heavy paths.
- Measurement noise: inter-node network jitter affected KV miss tail; next sweep should isolate KV RPC host locality.
- Synthetic workload approximates customer mix but lacks conversational multi-turn context which increases KV reuse; re-run with real session traces for verification.

Recommendations (short list):
1) Ship a small change to routing policy that exposes a cost/latency tier for customers and pins UI routes to micro-batch or batch=1. (owner: Product + Runtime)
2) Add a runtime metric: batching_wait_p95 per route, surfaced in Console. Alert when > configured threshold. (owner: observability)
3) Warm pool warmup: ensure model weight residency and lazy-JIT priming during low-traffic windows to reduce cold-start p99. (owner: infra)
4) KV locality: prioritize cached-shard routing for high-throughput routes to keep miss rate low; add instrumentation to separate local vs remote kv latencies. (owner: platform-engineering)
5) Run a follow-up stratified trace sweep using real-session traces (Leah to coordinate) and a finer batch_wait grid (5/10/15/25/40ms).

Trace quality and measurement caveats:
- Sampling bias: we used uniform sampling at ingress but heavy-tailed requests are rarer—need stratified sampling for long-seq heavy paths.

Appendix: quick checklist to reproduce
- config repo: runtime/benchmarks/batch-sweep-2026
- workload generator: tools/trace-synth (seeded with session-sample-2025-12)
- sampling: 10k per config over 1 hour, keep full trace payloads for 1 week

Raw notes and hypotheses we didn't confirm yet:
- Hypothesis: adaptive batching (short-circuiting when queue contains long-seqs) could salvage p95 while keeping throughput—needs model seq-length aware queue prioritization.
- Hypothesis: micro-bursts of egress network saturation coincide with KV miss spikes—investigate cross-tenant egress shaping.
